title: Money and paperwork
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE NUMBER RULE, at last. Russian counts in three shapes: 1 takes the NOMINATIVE SINGULAR (odín rubl'), 2, 3 and 4 take the GENITIVE SINGULAR (dva rublyá), and 5 and everything above takes the GENITIVE PLURAL (pyat' rubléy). The rule then restarts on the LAST DIGIT, so 21 goes back to odín rubl' and 22 to dva rublyá. L1-M8 shipped rubléy and chasóv without ever saying why; this is the why, and it explains both retroactively.

English has one plural and uses it after every number from two upwards — two roubles, five roubles, twenty-one roubles. Russian makes three choices instead of one, and makes them on the last digit rather than on the size of the number. A learner who picks one ending and sticks with it is wrong two times in three, which is why the rule is worth learning as arithmetic rather than as vocabulary.

Round hundreds and a thousand are the vocabulary that makes the rule usable: sto, dvésti, trísta, týsyacha. A rent or a salary is five digits and has to be said aloud, so these earn their room — but only the round ones. Everything between them is built from what L1-M8 already gave you, and the comprehension pool is where that practice belongs.

This module speaks vy from beginning to end, because a counter is exactly what that register was made for. Nothing new is opened for politeness: zapólnite and podpishíte are L2-M1's imperative, mózhno and nel'zyá are M4's, and pozháluysta is where it always was. That is what leaves the room for the numbers.

The vocabulary is simply what appears on the paper: schyot, kvitántsiya, arénda, dokumént, ankéta, pódpis', srok, nalóg. Each genitive shape a number frame needs lives in its own noun's forms rather than on a row of its own — sto týsyach rubléy is one phrase with two counted nouns in it, and both are the same rule.

words.note: Two hundred. It ends the number in a zero, so what follows is the genitive plural: dvésti rubléy. The rule reads the LAST digit and nothing else.

sentences.trap: rubléy is not a plural in the English sense — it is the genitive plural, and it appears because the number ends in 0.
sentences.sound: EH-ta STO-it DVYE-sti rub-LEY. dvésti keeps its stress at the front, rubléy at the very end.

variations.changed: 5 and up take the genitive plural

mistake.why: rublyá is the shape for 2, 3 and 4 only. Two hundred ends in a zero, so it is rubléy.

sentences.usage: Asking a price and understanding the answer.
sentences.mnemonic: One rubl', two rublyá, five rubléy — and 200 counts as none of them but the last.

sentences.cue: The rent is a hundred thousand roubles

words.note: The rent on a flat, as a sum rather than as an act. Paying it is platít' aréndu, in the accusative, and the word itself never changes its stress.
A thousand is týsyacha; after sto it becomes the genitive plural týsyach, and the roubles after it follow the same rule. Two counted nouns, one rule.

sentences.trap: Two counted nouns in a row, and the rule is applied twice: sto decides týsyach, and the whole number decides rubléy.
sentences.sound: a-RYEN-da STO-it sto TY-syach rub-LEY. týsyach is front-stressed and short.

variations.cue: The rent is two hundred thousand roubles

variations.changed: L1-M8's question, on a new noun

mistake.why: týsyachi is the shape after 2, 3 and 4. sto ends in a zero, so the genitive plural týsyach is what follows it.

sentences.usage: The first question about any flat, and the first number you have to hear correctly.
sentences.mnemonic: sto týsyach rubléy — the rule runs down the line.

sentences.cue: Three hundred roubles have to be paid

words.note: The finished act of paying. After nádo it stays an infinitive, exactly as after L2-M1's nádo — one form, and the person is left out or put in the dative.
Three hundred, front-stressed like dvésti. It ends in a zero, so the noun after it is the genitive plural: trísta rubléy.

sentences.trap: nádo takes an infinitive and no subject. Adding ya to it is the one thing that makes this sentence wrong.
sentences.sound: NA-da za-pla-TIT TRI-sta rub-LEY. The infinitive ending -tit' is short and unstressed at the end.

variations.cue: The bill has to be paid
variations.changed: L2-M5's bill, as the thing paid

variations.cue: It has to be paid today

mistake.why: nádo never takes a nominative. Either leave the person out or put them in the dative: mne nádo zaplatít'.

sentences.usage: Working out what is owed, aloud, in front of the person who is owed it.
sentences.mnemonic: nádo plus an infinitive — no one is named.

sentences.cue: Where can I pay the tax?

words.note: A tax, and the thing paid, so it stands in the accusative — which for this noun looks exactly like the plain form. Stress on the ending: na-LOG.

sentences.trap: mózhno needs no ya either. The question is about what is possible here, not about you.
sentences.sound: gdye MOZH-na za-pla-TIT na-LOK. The final g of nalóg is said as a k.

variations.cue: You can pay the tax here
variations.changed: the answer instead of the question
the object left out, as at a counter

mistake.why: mózhno is impersonal — there is no room for ya in it. The dative is the most it ever takes: mne mózhno.

sentences.usage: Standing in the wrong queue in a government office.
sentences.mnemonic: gde mózhno — where is it possible, not where can I.

words.note: L2-M1's polite imperative on a new verb: the -ite ending is the one in skazhíte and pomogíte. It is what you are told, not what you say.
The printed form with boxes on it. Accusative here because it is the thing filled in; on its own it is ankéta.

sentences.trap: ankéta is a form, not a questionnaire in the survey sense, and never a formality. It is the paper in front of you.
sentences.sound: za-POL-ni-tye an-KYE-tu, pa-ZHA-lu-sta. pozháluysta loses its middle: pa-ZHAL-sta in fast speech.

mistake.why: The form is the thing being filled in, so it takes the accusative: ankétu. The -a ending is the naming form only.

sentences.usage: The sentence every counter in the country says to you.
sentences.mnemonic: -ite is what they say to you; -u is what you do it to.

words.note: Signature, stressed on the first syllable: POD-pis'. It is feminine despite the consonant ending, which is why it takes vásha and not vash.

sentences.trap: A noun ending in -' can be either gender, and this one is feminine. vásha pódpis', never vash pódpis'.
sentences.sound: VA-sha POT-pis ZDYES. The d is said as a t before the p.

mistake.why: pódpis' is feminine, so the possessive is vásha. The soft sign at the end is the only clue, and it is not a reliable one — this word has to be learnt with its gender.

sentences.usage: A clerk pointing at the bottom of a page.
sentences.mnemonic: vásha pódpis' — feminine, whatever the ending looks like.

words.note: Any official paper, and in the plural dokuménty is what an official means by "your papers". Stress on the last syllable: do-ku-MENT.

sentences.trap: No moy in it. Losing it already says whose it was, and Russian leaves the possessive out.
sentences.sound: ya pa-ti-RYAL da-ku-MYENT. Both words put their weight on the last syllable.

variations.changed: a different paper, in the accusative

mistake.why: Grammatical, but nobody says it. The possessive is dropped wherever the owner is obvious.

sentences.usage: The worst sentence in the module, and the one you will need.
sentences.mnemonic: do-ku-MENT — the stress is at the end, as in English.

words.note: The slip that proves a payment, as against schyot, which is the bill asking for it. Stress in the middle: kvi-TAN-tsi-ya.

sentences.trap: yest' belongs here, unlike in the health module: the whole point is that the receipt exists and you are holding it.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA yest kvi-TAN-tsi-ya. The -iya ending runs together into one soft syllable.

variations.display: U menyá yest' kvitántsiya i dokumént
variations.script: У меня есть квитанция и документ
variations.cue: I have the receipt and the document

mistake.why: The verb exists and is used in contracts, not at a counter. Say u menyá yest'.

sentences.usage: Proving you have already paid, which happens more often than it should.

words.note: The date by which a thing must be done — a deadline, a term, a period of validity. One syllable, and no verb needed around it.

sentences.trap: There is no verb in the sentence, because Russian has no present tense of "to be". The two words are simply set beside each other.
sentences.sound: srok u-ZHE ZAF-tra. závtra is said with an f in the middle.

mistake.why: yest' says a thing exists. A deadline that falls tomorrow needs no verb at all.

sentences.usage: The line that decides whether today is calm or not.
sentences.mnemonic: Two nouns, no verb — Russian's present tense of "to be" is silence.

words.note: The instrumental — the case that means BY means of. It is L2-M2's ending on a new noun: kártoy for the card, and the plain form is kárta.

sentences.trap: No preposition. "By card" is one word in Russian, and the ending carries the "by".
sentences.sound: MOZH-na za-pla-TIT KAR-toy. The question is made by the rise at the end alone.

mistake.why: s is not needed and would take a different case anyway. The instrumental on its own means by this means: kártoy.

sentences.usage: Said at every till, several times a day.

comprehensionPool.cue: The rent is a hundred thousand roubles
Three hundred roubles have to be paid
Where can I pay the tax?
